title: Train, validation and test splits
summary: Judge a model only on data it never learned from. The training set fits the weights, the validation set chooses settings such as degree or λ, and the test set is opened once for an honest final estimate. Shuffle with a seed before splitting (but split time series by time), use k-fold cross-validation when data is scarce, and fit preprocessing on the training set only.
llm_link: Public benchmarks can leak into a language model's web-scale training text (contamination), so a model may score well partly by remembering test questions. Careful evaluations check for overlap or use fresh, held-back questions.
key_ideas: Training set: fit the weights. Validation set: choose settings (degree, λ, k, architecture). Test set: one final, honest estimate.
Every choice made by looking at a score leaks a little information. Tuning on the test set makes its score optimistic.
Shuffle before splitting, with a fixed seed so the split is repeatable. For time series, train on the past and test on later data.
k-fold cross-validation: rotate the validation fold through k parts and average the k scores.
Fit preprocessing (means, standard deviations, vocabularies) on the training set only, then apply the same numbers to validation and test.

quiz.q: You try 30 values of λ and pick the one with the best validation score. Which set gives an honest estimate of the chosen model's performance?
options: Any of them, since λ is just one number
quiz.explain: The validation score of the winner is biased upward, because it was selected for looking good on that data. Only data untouched by the selection (the test set) is honest.

quiz.q: Predict the result: 30 equally good settings each have true accuracy 80%, and each validation score is 80% ± random noise. What is the best validation score you will typically see?
quiz.explain: The maximum of 30 noisy scores sits above their common mean. That gap is pure luck, and it disappears on fresh data.

quiz.q: Your data is sorted by date and you want to predict next month's sales. How should you split?
options: Shuffle, then take a random 20% as test
Train on earlier dates, test on the latest dates
Use the earliest dates as the test set
Splitting does not matter for time series
quiz.explain: Shuffling would put future days in the training set, letting the model peek at tomorrow. Splitting by time mimics how the model will actually be used.

quiz.q: What is wrong with standardising features using the mean and standard deviation of the whole dataset before splitting?
options: The test set's values have influenced the training data, a subtle leak
quiz.explain: Compute μ and σ on the training set alone and apply those same numbers to validation and test, as if the test data arrived tomorrow.

quiz.q: A language model aces a public benchmark released three years before its training data was collected. What should you suspect first?
options: The benchmark is too easy for humans
Contamination: benchmark questions and answers may be in its training text
quiz.explain: Web-scale training data can contain published benchmarks. The model may partly be remembering rather than reasoning, so the score overstates its ability on new questions.

problems.title: A seeded three-way split
problems.prompt:
Write split_indices(n, val_frac, test_frac, seed) that shuffles the indices 0 … n−1 with np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(n) and cuts them into three arrays: train, validation, test. Use n_test = int(n * test_frac) and n_val = int(n * val_frac); the test indices come first in the shuffled order, then validation, and the rest are training.

The same seed must always give the same split, and no index may appear in two parts.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def split_indices(n, val_frac, test_frac, seed):
    perm = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(n)
    n_test = int(n * test_frac)
    n_val = int(n * val_frac)
    # TODO: slice perm into test, val and train (in that order)
    train = perm
    val = perm[:0]
    test = perm[:0]
    return train, val, test

tests.name: sizes
tests.code:
tr, va, te = split_indices(100, 0.2, 0.1, seed=0)
assert (len(tr), len(va), len(te)) == (70, 20, 10), f'expected 70/20/10, got {len(tr)}/{len(va)}/{len(te)}'

tests.name: no overlap, nothing lost
tests.code:
tr, va, te = split_indices(100, 0.2, 0.1, seed=0)
allidx = np.concatenate([tr, va, te])
assert len(set(allidx.tolist())) == 100 and sorted(allidx.tolist()) == list(range(100)), 'every index must appear in exactly one part; an overlap means the model is judged on data it learned from'

tests.name: repeatable
tests.code:
a = split_indices(50, 0.2, 0.2, seed=7); b = split_indices(50, 0.2, 0.2, seed=7)
assert all(np.array_equal(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)), 'the same seed must give the same split'

tests.name: actually shuffled
tests.code:
tr, va, te = split_indices(100, 0.2, 0.1, seed=0)
assert not np.array_equal(np.sort(te), np.arange(10)), 'the test set is just the first 10 rows: slice the shuffled perm, not range(n)'

problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def split_indices(n, val_frac, test_frac, seed):
    perm = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(n)
    n_test = int(n * test_frac)
    n_val = int(n * val_frac)
    test = perm[:n_test]
    val = perm[n_test:n_test + n_val]
    train = perm[n_test + n_val:]
    return train, val, test

tests.name: never in both in the same round

hints: train = np.concatenate([c for j, c in enumerate(chunks) if j != i])
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def kfold_indices(n, k):
    chunks = np.array_split(np.arange(n), k)
    folds = []
    for i in range(k):
        val = chunks[i]
        train = np.concatenate([c for j, c in enumerate(chunks) if j != i])
        folds.append((train, val))
    return folds

problems.title: Standardise without leaking
problems.prompt:
Write fit_scaler(X_train) that returns the column means and standard deviations of the training data (each of shape (d,), use axis=0), and transform(X, mu, sd) that returns (X − mu) / sd.

Shapes: X is (n, d) and mu is (d,), so broadcasting subtracts the mean of each column from every row.

tests.code:

Z = transform(X_train, mu, sd)
assert np.allclose(Z.mean(axis=0), 0) and np.allclose(Z.std(axis=0), 1), 'after transform, each training column should have mean 0 and sd 1'

tests.code:

Z = transform(X_test, mu, sd)
assert Z[:, 0].mean() > 0.2, 'the drifted test column should NOT come out with mean 0: transform must use the training mu and sd, not refit on the test data'

tests.name: fit_scaler only sees what it is given
tests.code:

assert np.allclose(mu, X_train.mean(axis=0)), 'the mean must come from X_train alone'
